clue.text: Parting shot to provoke interrupted by Republican mug

indicators.note: an interruption arrives in the middle of what it interrupts, so the letter named next lands inside

parts.note: to provoke someone is to stir them up
R is the standing short form for a Republican, as on a US ballot paper
a mug and a cup are the same vessel

explanation.surface: A departing insult meant to provoke, cut short by some Republican fool.
explanation.walkthrough: A stirrup cup is the drink handed up to a rider already in the saddle, a hunt-meeting custom. 'Mug' looks like the fool the surface is describing and wants the vessel instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A stirrup cup is drunk by someone on the point of riding off, so it is a shot taken at parting.

clue.text: No end to deception? Bank more responsible

indicators.note: the word loses its end, so its last letter goes

parts.note: guile is cunning deception
a tier is a bank, a row of seats or layers rising one above another

explanation.surface: Endless trickery leaves a bank more to blame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bank' looks like the financial villain of the surface but means a row or layer. 'No end to' cuts GUILE to GUIL.
explanation.definitionFit: Being guiltier means bearing more of the blame, so being more responsible for a wrong.

clue.text: Model that's short inspired with sexy pictures

indicators.note: a word given short is stopped before its end, so its final letter never arrives
to inspire is to breathe in, and what is breathed in ends up inside

parts.note: to model is to pose, docked here to POS
hot is the everyday word for sexy

explanation.surface: A model, briefly, who is fired up by racy pictures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model' is the verb, the thing done in front of a camera, not the person doing it. 'Inspired' passes as enthusiasm while quietly issuing the instruction to swallow something.
explanation.definitionFit: Photos are what a camera produces, the clipped plural of photographs that any set of pictures is made of.

clue.text: Newspaper plugging a column

indicators.note: a plug goes into the gap it fills, so whatever is plugging something sits inside it

parts.note: per means for each, as in twice a day
the i is a British daily paper, the compact spin-off of the Independent

explanation.surface: A newspaper plugging one of its own columns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plugging' reads as promotion, which is what a paper does for its columnists, and it is the insertion. A pier is the solid pillar carrying an arch or a bridge, not only the seaside walkway.
explanation.definitionFit: A pier is the masonry support that holds up an arch, which is a column in the builder's sense of the word.

clue.text: Any, perhaps put off by Tramp's ribaldry, initially?

parts.note: to deter is to put off
the setter, Tramp, refers to himself: Tramp's means mine

indicators.note: initially means take only the opening letter of ribaldry

explanation.surface: Is anyone deterred by the setter's bawdy humour?
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's own name stands for 'my' or 'mine'. In grammar a determiner is a word such as any, the or some placed before a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Any is an example of a determiner, the grammatical class of words that introduce a noun.

clue.text: Singer of core piece in heavy metal on tour

indicators.note: letters on tour move from place to place, so they do not stay in the order they were given
the core piece in a word is the single letter sitting dead centre of it

parts.note: the little word goes into the mix as it stands
hEAvy has five letters and A is the third
anagram fodder, five letters

explanation.surface: A singer taking the central number in a heavy metal band's touring set.
explanation.walkthrough: Grammar words are fodder too: 'of' hands over two of the eight letters while looking like nothing at all. Meat Loaf was the stage name of the American rock singer who recorded Bat Out of Hell.
explanation.definitionFit: Meat Loaf was the working name of Michael Lee Aday, whose Bat Out of Hell is one of the best-selling albums ever made.

clue.text: More sentimental movie occasionally entertained by promiscuous type

indicators.note: a guest entertained by a host is taken indoors, and these letters go inside the word named after them

parts.note: a goer is British slang for someone keen on sex

indicators.note: what happens occasionally happens now and then rather than throughout, so every other letter is taken

parts.note: every other letter of mOvIe

explanation.surface: The occasional film enjoyed by someone who puts it about.
explanation.walkthrough: The host is named second here, so the alternate letters are the guests and go in the middle. Gooey has slid from treacle to sentimentality, and this is its comparative.
explanation.definitionFit: A gooier film is a stickier, more sugary one, gooey doing for feelings what it does for toffee.

clue.text: Fix gates having lost a sheep

indicators.note: to fix the gates is to rework them, so their letters are rearranged
the letter a is lost from the rearranged pool

explanation.surface: A farmer repairing broken gates after a sheep has got out.
explanation.walkthrough: GATES without its A is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A teg is a sheep in its second year, a dialect word for a yearling.

clue.text: Tuchel on playing over one side of pitch

indicators.note: playing suggests the letters are moving about in play, so they are rearranged

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Thomas Tuchel, the football manager, prowls one side of the pitch during a game.
explanation.walkthrough: TUCHEL ON is mixed with I, which the anagram takes in.
explanation.definitionFit: The touchline is the boundary marking each long side of a football or rugby pitch.

clue.text: Eat in bar filling beer out of case

indicators.note: whatever fills something goes inside it, into the space it takes up
a case is the outside of a thing, so out of its case a word loses the letters at each end

parts.note: bEEr with the B and R of its case taken off
a rod is a bar of metal

explanation.surface: Eating at the bar while the beer comes out of its case.
explanation.walkthrough: A case of beer is what the surface offers and a case of letters is what the clue means, the two at each end. 'Eat' is erosion in the sense of a river eating at its bank.
explanation.definitionFit: Water erodes a bank by eating it away, and eat carries exactly that sense of wearing a thing down bit by bit.

clue.text: One tells Romeo to come back for coffee first

indicators.note: first says this letter goes ahead of the following piece

parts.note: R is Romeo in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: back for means the last letter of the word coffee is taken

parts.note: something still to come happens later

explanation.surface: Someone tells their lover to come back for coffee before anything else.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who recounts a story or narrates events is one who tells.

clue.text: Admissions with nurse getting samples

parts.note: EN is an enrolled nurse, the rank below a registered one on a British ward
to try a dish is to sample it

explanation.surface: A hospital admissions desk where the nurse is taking samples.
explanation.walkthrough: The hospital sentence hides two ordinary words: the nurse is an abbreviation and the samples are a verb. EN for nurse is one to stock, along with SEN and RN.
explanation.definitionFit: An entry is an admission in both senses the word carries — being let in, and the line written down when you are.

clue.text: Forces American to accept idiot

indicators.note: what a word accepts it takes in and keeps inside itself

parts.note: US is the standing short form for American
a nit is a fool in British usage, the insult behind nitwit

explanation.surface: An American being made to put up with a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forces' reads as the verb driving the sentence and is wanted as the noun: the units an army is divided into. Nit belongs to a family of mild British insults that crosswords keep in circulation.
explanation.definitionFit: Army units are the separate forces a commander has to send out, so one plural noun stands for the other.

clue.text: Scan, mark and tick in school going over stuff

indicators.note: in means the mark and tick go inside the school word
going over means turning over, so the school word is read backwards

parts.note: a gam is a school of whales
M is the abbreviation for mark, the old German currency
a mo, or tick, is a moment
to ram is to stuff or cram

explanation.surface: A teacher marks and ticks work in school, going over the material.
explanation.walkthrough: 'school' suggests a classroom, matching the teacher's marking in the surface, but here it is a school of whales, a gam, which 'going over' turns round.
explanation.definitionFit: A mammogram is an X-ray image of the breast used in screening, so a type of medical scan.

clue.text: They shot once in game with forwards

definitions.note: The definition describes the things rather than naming them: these are guns that did the shooting in their day, and 'once' does the dating.

parts.note: a match is a game between two sides
the locks are the two second-row forwards in a rugby union pack

explanation.surface: Players who managed a single shot in a game with the forwards.
explanation.walkthrough: A matchlock fired when a burning cord — the match — was lowered into the powder, which is where the weapon and the fixture share a word. Locks are the tall pair in the second row of a rugby scrum.
explanation.definitionFit: Matchlocks were the muskets of the sixteenth century, long since superseded, so their shooting was all done once upon a time.

clue.text: They might have finished second drink, primarily restricted by menus?

indicators.note: what restricts a thing closes round it and holds it in

parts.note: a menu is a list of meals, so menus are meal lists

indicators.note: what comes primarily comes first, so only the opening letter of the word is wanted

parts.note: the opening letter of drink

explanation.surface: People who saw off a second drink, limited by what the menus offered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finished second' is about silver, not about a second helping. The question mark is the setter owning up to his two-word reading of menus, which is where the long chunk of letters comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: Medals go to the first three home, so anyone who finished second has one hanging round their neck.

clue.text: Sort out clothing for catholic girlfriend: something to cover boobs in work?

definitions.text: something to cover boobs in work

indicators.note: to sort a heap is to put it into a different order, which is what becomes of these letters

parts.note: anagram fodder, three letters

indicators.note: clothing is what goes on the outside, so a word's clothing is the letter at each of its ends

parts.note: the clothing of catholiC is its first and last letters
anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: Sorting out what to wear for a catholic girlfriend.
explanation.walkthrough: Boobs are blunders here and work is what you typed, so the cover is the white stuff brushed over a mistake. 'Sort' alone is the instruction — 'out' has been quietly recruited as fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Correcting fluid is the white paint dabbed over an error on a typed or written page, and a boob is a British word for a blunder.

clue.text: Use team with changes to draw in league matches

indicators.note: a side that makes changes does not field the same players in the same places, and nor do these letters
to draw something in is to pull it inside, so the letter named joins the rest

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
l is the standing short form for league, as in the league tables

explanation.surface: A manager using the team with changes to force a draw in a league fixture.
explanation.walkthrough: The football sentence is seamless and every part of it is an instruction: the changes, the drawing in, the league. 'Matches' is the verb — to emulate a rival is to match what they did.
explanation.definitionFit: To emulate someone is to match them, equalling what they achieved, so one third-person verb stands for the other.

clue.text: Have erred cracking Paul cryptic leading to confusion

indicators.note: the first set of letters breaks into the second, sitting inside them
cryptic means puzzling and hidden, so the letters of Paul are jumbled
something that has erred has gone astray, so the letters of have are mixed up

explanation.surface: Someone confesses a mistake in solving a Paul cryptic, ending in confusion.
explanation.walkthrough: Paul is a fellow Guardian setter, and 'cryptic' looks like it describes his puzzle, but it is the signal to jumble his name; 'erred' and 'cracking' do the other two jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: An upheaval is a violent disturbance or disruption, a state of turmoil and confusion.

clue.text: Life around north: show one with boring job

indicators.note: what goes around something closes on it from both sides

parts.note: pep is life in the sense of energy and go
n is the standing short form for north, as on a map
to show someone to their seat is to usher them

explanation.surface: Life up north, put on show for someone stuck in a dull job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Show' is the verb that hides a person: the one who shows you in at a theatre door. A pen-pusher is the clerk who spends the day shifting paper, and the phrase carries a sneer.
explanation.definitionFit: A pen-pusher does routine clerical work, which is the dull job the definition means, with mild contempt attached.

clue.text: Figure in a dress?

definitions.meaning: the arithmetical sense, a figure written down on a page
a frock, in the throwaway way a shop assistant might name one

explanation.surface: A shapely figure inside a dress.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves of this very short clue are definitions and no letters move anywhere. The article belongs to the second one: it is 'a number' a dress gets called, never 'number' on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: A number is a figure in the arithmetical sense, and a number is also a garment — the little black number of the shop floor.

clue.text: Doctor from department parking by hospital on single line

parts.note: d is the short form of department, as in a departmental heading
P is the letter on every British parking sign
H is the hospital sign on a British road
I is one in Roman numerals, and a single is one
l is the standing short form for line

explanation.surface: A doctor from the department parking by the hospital on a single yellow line.
explanation.walkthrough: Five abbreviations in a row and the surface still reads as a sentence about a hospital car park. A DPhil is what Oxford calls the doctorate other universities award as a PhD.
explanation.definitionFit: A DPhil is a doctorate, the degree whose holder is entitled to be called doctor, awarded under that name at Oxford and Sussex.

clue.text: Clear religious person is bored by mass

indicators.note: to bore is to drill a hole right through, so the letter named lands in the middle

parts.note: a deist believes in a creator known from reason rather than from revelation
m is the physicist's symbol for mass

explanation.surface: A religious man bored stiff by the Mass.
explanation.walkthrough: Mass with a capital is the church service the surface leans on; mass in lower case is the letter physics uses. 'Clear' is what you do to a windscreen on a cold morning.
explanation.definitionFit: To demist glass is to clear the film of condensation off it, so both words name the same act on a windscreen.

clue.text: Release album: sound issue with disc, perhaps?

indicators.note: to release something is to let it go free, and letters let go settle in a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, five letters
when a bell sounds we say it goes

explanation.surface: Putting out an album, and the trouble with the sound on the disc.
explanation.walkthrough: The record-shop surface hides a waiting room: the disc is the one in your spine and the issue is a bad back. 'Sound' is not asking for a homophone — it wants a word meaning to go.
explanation.definitionFit: Lumbago is pain in the lower back, commonly blamed on a slipped spinal disc, so the definition names it by a likely cause.

clue.text: They kiss with small tablet, shortly getting erect

indicators.note: in a down light, standing upright means the letters are read from the bottom upwards
shortly cuts the last letter from the word

parts.note: a pill is a tablet
S is the clothing-size abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: A cheeky line about a little pill and its effects on a couple.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a joke about a certain blue pill; 'getting erect' actually turns the shortened PILL upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The mouth's soft edges are what meet in a kiss, so they are what kisses.

clue.text: Cut chicken to eat roast; they have skins on top

indicators.note: to eat means the shortened word takes the other inside it
cut removes the final letter

parts.note: chicken means timid, cowardly
to roast is to criticise harshly, to pan

explanation.surface: Carve a chicken so it can take in some roasting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'chicken' and 'roast' look like cooking; they are timid and criticise.
explanation.definitionFit: Kettledrums have stretched membranes, called skins or heads, across their top.

clue.text: Lorry driver finally going for food

indicators.note: finally points at the end of a word, so only the last letter is meant
what is going leaves, and the letter named goes out of the word

parts.note: a truck is a lorry
the last letter of driveR

explanation.surface: A lorry driver pulling in at the end of a run for something to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lorry driver' reads as one man and is two instructions: the lorry gives the word, the driver gives the letter taken out of it. Tuck is British schoolboy food, the buns and sweets of the tuck shop.
explanation.definitionFit: Tuck is food in the British school sense — what the tuck shop sells and what a tuck box is packed with.

clue.text: Man that could be a hunk

definitions.meaning: the chessboard sense of man, one of the sixteen a player pushes about
a lump broken off something larger, as in a hunk of bread

explanation.surface: A man who might just turn out to be a hunk.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface leans on the admiring hunk, the one at the gym, while the clue means the lump of cheese. 'Man' is the chess word, which is why the definition can be singular and human at once.
explanation.definitionFit: A chessman is a piece, and a hunk of bread is a piece of it, so both halves are the same plain noun in different company.

clue.text: Set off with Tom after thrills

indicators.note: what comes after a thing is written behind it, so the piece named first ends up second

parts.note: kicks are thrills, as in doing something for kicks
tom is British slang for a prostitute, and so is tart

explanation.surface: Setting off with Tom once the excitement has died down.
explanation.walkthrough: Tom reads as a name and is slang: the British police and papers have used it for a prostitute for decades. To kick-start a scheme is to get it going with one shove, as a motorbike pedal does.
explanation.definitionFit: To kick-start something is to set it off, the phrase coming from the pedal that fires a motorbike engine into life.
